title: Pneumonia, Bacterial

content_blocks.text: Acquired inflammatory response to bacteria in lung parenchyma characterized by exudation of cells and fluid into conducting airways and alveolar spaces.
Bacteria—enter the lower respiratory tract primarily by inhalation or aspiration; less commonly by the hematogenous route. Infection incites an inflammatory reaction.

Inpatient—recommended with multisystemic signs (e.g., anorexia, fever) or in patients with respiratory compromise in the absence of multisystemic signs.

Physical therapy— chest wall coupage, tracheal manipulation to stimulate mild cough and postural drainage; may enhance clearance of secretions; always do immediately after nebulization; avoid allowing the patient to lie in one position for a prolonged time.
Oxygen therapy—as warranted for patients with hypoxemia, signs of respiratory distress.

Antitussives—potent, centrally acting agents inhibit mucokinesis and exudate removal from airways; can potentiate pulmonary infection and inflammation.

Prognosis—good with aggressive antibacterial and supportive therapy; more guarded in young animals, patients with immunodeficiency, and patients that are debilitated or have severe
Prolonged infection— potential for chronic bronchitis or bronchiectasis
Mortality—associated with severe hypoxemia and sepsis.

Frequently develops secondary to underlying functional or anatomic abnormalities—cleft palate; tracheal hypoplasia; primary ciliary dyskinesia; laryngeal paralysis; megaesophagus or other esophageal dysmotility disorder.
